sections.h2: Where do you record a deed in Wayne County, PA?
sections.html:
At the Recorder of Deeds office in the Wayne County Courthouse Annex, 925 Court Street, Honesdale, PA 18431. The phone is 570-253-5970, extension 4040. The office is open Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and nothing is accepted for recording after 4:00 p.m.

Wayne County calls the office the custodian of the records and indexes for land transfers. It keeps deeds, mortgages, subdivision plans, rights-of-way and easements, and it also records the commissions and oaths of county officials, district justices and notaries, plus military discharges. A house sale in Wayne County ends here: after closing, the signed deed is recorded in Honesdale, and the new owner appears in the public record from that point.

The county asks one thing of readers up front. Staff cannot give legal advice or attorney referrals, so questions about how to word a deed belong with a lawyer, and the Wayne County Bar Association keeps a member list.

sections.h2: What new Uniform Parcel Identifier rule started in Wayne County in November 2026?
sections.html:
UPI certification began on November 2, 2026, at $20.00 per UPI number. The county posted the start date and the fee at the top of its recorder page, and its tax sale page notes that the Wayne County UPI Ordinance was adopted, with a $20.00 fee for each Uniform Parcel Identifier beginning that date.

For a seller, the practical effect is simple. A deed for a parcel now involves a certification step, and a sale that covers more than one parcel pays the $20.00 once per UPI number. Ask the recorder's office for the UPI notice, and have your closing agent or attorney confirm when the certification has to be completed.

The same date changed another number. The county's tax sale page says the deed recording fee became $94.75 as of November 2, 2026. That figure appears in the context of a tax sale deed, so ask the office to confirm the charge for an ordinary private sale deed.

sections.h2: What charges does Wayne County name on its recorder and tax sale pages?
sections.html:
Wayne County posts a fee schedule as a spreadsheet and a PDF, and the figures below are the ones stated on the county's web pages themselves.

For a plain deed, the county's page does not print one total, so call 570-253-5970, extension 4040, or open the fee schedule on the county's Recorder of Deeds page. The schedule is dated November 2026, and it lists fees by document type.

sections.h2: How can a Wayne County deed be e-recorded?
sections.html:
Through one of two vendors: CSC at 866-652-0111 or Simplifile at 800-460-5657. Most land-related documents can be sent that way without a trip to Honesdale.

Two kinds of document cannot be e-recorded and must be delivered on paper: subdivision plans, and deeds that are taxable in more than one jurisdiction. The second exception comes up when a parcel lies in more than one municipality: the deed then has to state the percentage in each so the local transfer tax divides correctly.

  • E-recorded transactions with a REV-183 Statement of Value attach helper pages, and those pages cost $0.50 each.
  • Paper filings go to the courthouse annex before the 4:00 p.m. cutoff.
  • Faxed or emailed copies are not accepted for recording.

sections.h2: What does the Wayne County recorder require on a deed?
sections.html:
The county publishes a checklist, and it is stricter than many sellers expect. An acknowledgment must show the county, state, date, the people or corporate officers appearing, and the notary's signature, stamp and expiration date. If any of those is missing, the acknowledgment is treated as defective.

  • The written amount of consideration has to match the number on the deed.
  • Every deed, mortgage and assignment needs a signed certification of the grantee's address with zip code.
  • Transfer taxes or a completed Statement of Value must accompany every deed.
  • Black ink and white or manila paper only, since the office scans everything.
  • Documents may not exceed 8 1/2 by 14 inches, and maps may not exceed 24 by 36 inches.
  • Recorded papers come back by mail only if you enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

sections.h2: What is Wayne County like for a house sale?
sections.html:
It is a rural, lake-and-hill county in the Poconos with a small population. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 51,703 people on about 726 square miles of land, which works out to roughly 70 people per square mile. The county was formed in 1798 from part of Northampton County, and Honesdale is both the seat and the largest borough.

QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 shows 80.5 percent owner-occupancy, a median owner-occupied home value of $242,100, median gross rent of $1,038 and median household income of $62,381. Residents aged 65 or older make up 27.2 percent of the population, which is high, and 32,637 housing units serve only 20,877 households.

The county's boroughs are Bethany, Hawley, Honesdale, Prompton, Starrucca and Waymart. Terrain varies from rugged ground along the New York border to a wide central plain, and the Delaware River separates the county from New York. Winters are cold, with Honesdale averaging about 22.8 degrees in January, so heating systems and roofs draw attention at inspection. Six school districts serve the county: Forest City Regional, North Pocono, Susquehanna Community, Wallenpaupack Area, Wayne Highlands and Western Wayne.

sections.h2: What should a Wayne County seller know about assessments and unpaid taxes?
sections.html:
The Assessment Office maintains property records and prepares the tax rolls, and it does not set millage rates or collect taxes. It sits at 925 Court Street in Honesdale, phone 570-253-5970, extension 4010, open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The county has 28 municipalities and 6 school districts, all of which draw on those rolls.

Back taxes go to the Tax Claim Bureau, extension 4000, at the same address. It runs sales under the Real Estate Tax Sale Law, and unsold properties go on a repository list. Repository sales are held quarterly in February, May, August and November, and the owner can pay up to the day of the sale. Buyers at a repository sale pay costs, a $25 deed preparation fee and 2 percent transfer tax, and Act 33 requires every bidder to pre-register.

If a back-tax balance sits on the house you want to sell, ask the Tax Claim Bureau for a payoff figure before closing.

faqs.q: What are the Wayne County Recorder of Deeds hours?
faqs.a: The office is open Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., but it takes no documents for recording after 4:00 p.m. It is in the Courthouse Annex at 925 Court Street in Honesdale, and the phone is 570-253-5970, extension 4040.

faqs.q: Is there a new fee for parcel identifiers in Wayne County?
faqs.a: Yes. Uniform Parcel Identifier certification began on November 2, 2026, and costs $20.00 per UPI number. The county's recorder page links a UPI notice that explains the process.

faqs.q: Can I e-record a Wayne County deed?
faqs.a: Yes, with exceptions. Use CSC (866-652-0111) or Simplifile (800-460-5657). Subdivision plans and deeds taxable in multiple jurisdictions cannot be e-recorded and must go in on paper.

faqs.q: Does Wayne County mail back a recorded deed?
faqs.a: Only if you enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope when you submit it. Without one, the Recorder's Office does not mail recorded documents.

faqs.q: Where do I see who owns a Wayne County parcel?
faqs.a: Search recorded documents on Landex, which the county uses for online records. Index searching is free, and you pay only when you buy copies of documents to download or print.
